Instead, he journeyed to Kamakura, and sought apprenticeship with Shintogo Kunimitsu, then the most revered tsurugi-smith in the east. He needed power to smite the wicked. Only a tsurugi could grant him that. His advances were rebuffed, however. Tsurugi-smithing was a sacred art, to be passed from parent to child and none other. Kunimitsu would not teach a man who shared no common blood. Besides, the man was too old. Most tsurugi-smiths began their training from the day they could walk. Never had one begun so late. And finally, he was but Yamatoan, not an Emishi born to the forge. Even if he learned their arts, any tsurugi he forged would be inferior. So judged Kunimitsu, and so judged Kunimitsu's peers and disciples. They met the blacksmith with laughter and jeers, and perhaps with a flicker of fear in their faces; for the man's eyes shone with a light not wholly sane, and he spoke of naught but demons and the death he would deliver them. Salvation came from a direction nobody expected. Each school of tsurugi-
smithing passes its knowledge from parent to child. When the child has learned all that the parent can teach, the parent commits their soul to the forge. This has always been the way. However, this way carries risks. Should an accident befall the successor, for example, the secrets of the school may be lost, for the old master is now but silent metal, and cannot teach another. In order to prevent such tragedies, clans select one disciple―often the youngest
―in each generation to become the guardian of the line. This smith does not forge a tsurugi, but lives out his days teaching those who come after and ensuring that their secrets are not forgotten. When Kunimitsu's disciples rose to grab the blacksmith and fling him frothing from their gates, it was Kunimitsu's uncle, guardian of the Shintogo line, who intervened. He bade them show their guest to his chambers, and there, he addressed the blacksmith thus― "Truly, you are a tsurugi-
smith born. I have prepared many kinsmen for the forge. For most, it is a labor of many years. But it will not be so for you." The old smith was wise indeed, for tsurugi-smithing is the art of transmuting one's self into a stronger form. It requires a consummate understanding of one's nature and one's Way. This man already knew the shape of his soul, and the purpose to which he would bend his art. Thus this human, this lowly toolsmith, already possessed what it took most Emishi their whole lives to obtain.
